study.title: Jeremiah 28 The confrontation between the true word and the false word
study.overview: Jeremiah 28 records a public shock between Jeremiah and Hananiah, a prophet who promised rapid deliverance from Judah and the return of the temple and exiles. The chapter shows that not every religious message that sounds encouraging comes from the Lord. Jeremiah's answer is firm, but not aggressive: he desires that the promise of peace be true, but remembers that the truthfulness of a prophet proves by the fulfillment of the word. When Hananiah breaks the yoke of Jeremiah, the LORD responds with another symbolic image: instead of a yoke of broken wood, an iron yoke will come. The chapter ends with the death of Hananias in the same year, confirming that he spoke without divine commission.

outline.title: Hananias announces release in two years
outline.explanation: Hananiah confronts Jeremiah in the temple and states, in the name of the LORD, that the dominion of Babylon will be broken quickly, with the return of the sacred vessels and the exiles. The text makes it clear that its message circulates before priests and people, in an environment of strong public impact.

outline.title: Jeremiah desires good, but testes the prophecy
outline.explanation: Jeremiah responds with a sincere desire that the promise be fulfilled, but appeals to the prophetic tradition: old true messages announced judgment, not only peace. Hananias then breaks Jeremiah's yoke as a dramatic sign, reinforcing his prediction of rapid liberation.

outline.title: The Divine sentence against the false prophet
outline.explanation: After the theatrical gesture of Hananias, the LORD speaks again through Jeremiah. The symbol is inverted: from wooden yogars to iron yogs, indicating more severe servitude. Jeremiah denounces Hananiah's lie and announces his death later that year; the closure confirms the trial.

study.context: The chapter takes place at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah in the fourth year, fifth month. The notes indicate that the setting is the temple, with the assembled people, perhaps during an annual feast, but this is a possibility, not a certainty of the text. The conflict also presupposes the situation of Judah under the rule of Babylon, after 597 before Christ, when the message of submission to Nebuchadnezzar was unpopular.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that prophetic authority does not depend on a confident tone or impressive signs, but on the true commission of God and the fulfillment of the announced word. The truth of God may include prolonged judgment, and not just immediate relief. Jeremiah does not manipulate the hope of the people; he submits his expectation to the confirmation of the LORD. Hananiah, in promising peace without divine support, leads the people to trust lies. His death functions as judgment and also as confirmation that God continues to rule history and unmask false messengers. There is still a serious principle: speaking in the name of God without being sent by him is rebellion against the Lord himself.

scholarViews.insight: The scene takes place in the temple, before the people, as a public confrontation; the note also suggests that the date may coincide with an annual autumn feast.
Jeremiah does not oppose for pride: he desires that the word of Hananiah be fulfilled, but calls for the test of historical achievement to distinguish the true from the false prophet.
The death of Hananiah in the seventh month, after the prophecy was given in the fifth month, functions as a divine seal on Jeremiah's word and proof that Hananiah spoke without commission.

questions: How can we discern today between a spiritually attractive message and a word actually sent by God?
Why can Jeremiah desire that Hananiah's promise be true, but still reject it as false?
How does the history of this chapter correct our tendency to prefer quick answers instead of God's truth?
study.practice: Read carefully any religious teaching that promises an immediate solution, and compare it with the character of God and the whole of Scripture. Learn from Jeremiah not to react with vanity or anxiety, but with submission to the truth. When the message of God is difficult, do not soften it to please people; when correction is necessary, speak with firmness and humility. Also examine your own words: it is possible to use religious language and still lead people to trust in lies. The chapter calls the church to value above popularity allegiance.
study.uncertainty: The text does not explicitly inform that the occasion was a specific party; this appears only as a possibility in the notes. It is also not possible to state with certainty, only from this chapter, all the external historical details suggested by the commentators. The confessional readings presented here are evangelical interpretations of the text, not absolute statements other than what the chapter allows.
